question:
The predictive ability of a polygenic score, measured by variance explained, is necessarily lower than the SNP heritability for the phenotype. Answer with one of the following:
True
False

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP heritability of a phenotype represents the total proportion of variance that can be explained (in principle) by an optimal linear combination of the SNPs. A polygenic score is itself a linear combination of SNPs; with perfect effect-size estimates (i.e., in the infinite-data limit) its R² therefore reaches, but does not exceed, the SNP heritability. The inequality is therefore not strict, so the claim that predictive ability is “necessarily lower” is false.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) represents the total fraction of phenotypic variance that is (in principle) capturable by the set of SNPs when their true effect sizes are known. A polygenic score is a finite-sample estimator of those effect sizes; consequently its out-of-sample \(R^2\) is bounded above by \(h^2_{SNP}\) and is strictly smaller whenever any estimation error, imperfect LD tagging, or population mismatch remains. Hence the predictive ability “is necessarily lower.”

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability estimate captures the total proportion of phenotypic variance that can be attributed to the additive effects of all SNPs (typically via methods like GREML or LD score regression). In contrast, a polygenic score is derived from finite-sample GWAS summary statistics and therefore incorporates only imperfectly estimated effect sizes, incomplete variant coverage, and imperfect tagging of causal variants due to LD structure. These practical limitations mean the out-of-sample variance explained by the PGS cannot reach the SNP-heritability ceiling, so it is necessarily lower.

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is the proportion of phenotypic variance captured by the set of SNPs (i.e., the theoretical upper bound on additive genetic variance explainable by those markers). A polygenic score is a finite-sample, noisy estimator of the same additive effects; even when all SNPs are included and modern shrinkage methods are used, estimation error, imperfect LD tagging, and winner’s-curse bias ensure that the out-of-sample \(R^2\) attained by the score is strictly less than \(h^2_{SNP}\). Equality is reached only in the unattainable limit of infinite, perfectly measured data. Hence the predictive ability of any realizable polygenic score is necessarily lower than the SNP heritability.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is the proportion of phenotypic variance captured by the additive effects of all SNPs (i.e., \(\mathrm{Var}(X\beta)/\mathrm{Var}(y)\)). A polygenic score \(\hat{G}=X\hat{\beta}\) is simply an estimator of that same additive genetic component. When the GWAS sample size tends to infinity, \(\hat{\beta}\to\beta\) (under standard regularity conditions and correct model specification), so the out-of-sample \(R^2\) of the PGS converges to \(h^2_{SNP}\). Therefore the inequality is not strict; equality is attainable in the limit and the statement is false.

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

SNP heritability represents the total proportion of phenotypic variance that is tagged by (or attributable to) all measured SNPs. A polygenic score constructed from the true effect sizes of every SNP (i.e., in the theoretical limit of infinite GWAS sample size, perfect estimation, and no pruning) would therefore capture exactly that quantity and explain an equal amount of variance in an independent sample. In practice the realized R² is lower because of estimation error, but the statement claims the inequality is “necessarily” true; that is not the case, so the answer is false.

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP-based heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the proportion of phenotypic variance captured by an optimal linear combination of the SNPs (i.e., the population \(R^2\) of the best possible additive predictor built from those markers). Any concrete polygenic score is constructed from effect-size estimates obtained in a finite sample; those estimates contain noise, so the out-of-sample \(R^2\) achieved by the resulting score is strictly smaller than \(h^2_{SNP}\). Equality is attained only in the theoretical limit of infinite GWAS sample size, which is never realized in practice. Hence the predictive ability of a polygenic score is necessarily lower than SNP heritability.

8.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP-heritability of a phenotype is defined as the fraction of phenotypic variance that is tagged by the set of SNPs used in the analysis; it is therefore an upper bound on the out-of-sample variance that any linear predictor constructed from those SNPs can explain. With infinite GWAS sample size, perfect LD information, and a well-calibrated Bayesian shrinkage method that uses all SNPs, the polygenic score converges to this bound, so equality is attainable in the theoretical limit. The claim that the predictive R² is “necessarily lower” is therefore incorrect.

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the proportion of phenotypic variance captured by the best linear predictor that uses all SNPs jointly. A polygenic score, however, is constructed from finite-sample GWAS estimates of those SNP effects. Because the estimated weights contain sampling error (and usually additional shrinkage or pruning), the out-of-sample \(R^2\) achieved by any practical PGS is strictly less than \(h^2_{SNP}\). Only in the unattainable limit of infinite GWAS data would the two quantities coincide; under all realistic conditions the inequality is therefore necessary.

Final answer: True

Hence the predictive ability is necessarily lower than the SNP heritability.

11.text:

SNP heritability (h²_SNP) is the total proportion of phenotypic variance that can be linearly explained by the set of SNPs (i.e., the variance of the additive genetic component g = Xβ). A polygenic score is itself a linear combination of the same SNPs (PGS = Xβ̂). Because β̂ is estimated from finite data, it necessarily differs from the true β; the out-of-sample R² achieved by the PGS is therefore strictly less than h²_SNP. Equality is possible only in the theoretical limit of infinite, perfectly matched samples—an unattainable condition in any real analysis. Hence the predictive ability of any PGS, measured by variance explained, is necessarily lower than SNP heritability.

Hence the predictive ability of a PGS is necessarily lower than the SNP heritability.

13.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: True. The SNP heritability represents the total proportion of phenotypic variance that can be explained by all SNPs together when their effects are known without error. In contrast, a polygenic score is constructed from effect-size estimates obtained in a finite discovery sample, which necessarily introduces shrinkage, noise, and imperfect tagging of causal variants. As a result, the out-of-sample variance explained by even the best polygenic score is always strictly lower than the SNP heritability of the trait.

14.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability represents the total proportion of phenotypic variance that can be attributed to all SNPs in aggregate, which serves as an upper theoretical bound. However, a polygenic score is constructed from a finite set of estimated effect sizes derived from a GWAS sample. Even with large discovery samples, factors such as imperfect linkage disequilibrium between tagging SNPs and causal variants, winner’s curse in effect-size estimates, and incomplete capture of rare or structural variants mean that the out-of-sample R² achieved by any PGS will necessarily fall short of the SNP-heritability estimate. Therefore the statement holds.

15.text:

A polygenic score, however, is constructed from estimated effect sizes obtained in a finite discovery sample. Only in the theoretical limit of infinite discovery-sample size would equality be reached; under all realistic conditions the inequality is therefore strict. Hence the statement is true.
